sessions.title: Introduction & Foundations
sessions.goal: identify the core AI design principles that make AI-native products different from traditional software
sessions.preMaterials: Watch the Figma AI deep-dive (15 min, linked in resources). Come ready to name one thing that surprised you and one thing that felt half-baked.

sections.title: Check-in
sections.content: Go around: each person says in one sentence what she did since last time.

sections.title: Last week's task
sections.content: First session — no task yet. Quick round of introductions instead: name, role, and one thing you want to get from this Bubble.

sections.title: Learn
sections.content: Walk through what makes an AI-native product different from traditional software: latency as UX, probabilistic outputs, and progressive trust. Three live product examples — one that handles all three well, two that don't.

sections.title: Discuss
sections.content: Pairs: pick one AI product you use every week. Where does it feel intentionally designed? Where does it feel like the AI was bolted on? 10 minutes, then share one finding with the group.

sections.title: Wrap-up
sections.content: Agree on the task for next time and who leads the next session.

sessions.homework: Map one AI product you use daily: a screenshot, what the AI actually does, where it surprises you, and one specific thing you'd change. Bring it as a screenshot + 3 bullet points to share at the start of session 2.

sessions.title: Core Concepts Deep Dive
sessions.goal: explain the key frameworks from this program and apply one to a real product example
sessions.preMaterials: Read the NN/g article "Designing AI: The UX of Machine Learning" (10 min, linked). Annotate one thing you agree with and one thing you'd push back on.

sections.title: Check-in
sections.content: Go around: each person says in one sentence what she did since last time.

sections.title: Last week's task
sections.content: Whoever submitted shows her product map. Two minutes each — screenshot on screen, walk through the three bullet points. One comment from the group after each.

sections.title: Learn
sections.content: Go deeper on the three concepts from session 1. Latency: how Vercel's AI toolbar uses skeleton states and streaming to make 3-second waits feel fast. Probabilistic outputs: how Notion AI surfaces uncertainty without breaking flow. Progressive trust: how GitHub Copilot earns the right to autocomplete more over time.

sections.title: Discuss
sections.content: Which of the three concepts shows up most in your own work right now? Pairs share a specific moment — a screen, a flow, a edge case — where it mattered or caused a problem.

sections.title: Wrap-up
sections.content: Agree on the task for next time and who leads the next session.

sessions.homework: Pick one of the three concepts and find it in a product you work on or use regularly. Document what the product does well, where it breaks down, and one concrete change. Share as a Loom or annotated slide.

sessions.title: Practical Frameworks
sessions.goal: choose the right framework for a given design challenge and justify the choice to the group
sessions.preMaterials: Pick one product from your portfolio that has any AI or automation. Write 2 sentences: what does the AI do, and what does the user have to trust?

sections.title: Check-in
sections.content: Go around: each person says in one sentence what she did since last time.

sections.title: Last week's task
sections.content: Whoever submitted shows her Loom or slide. Two minutes, then one comment. Focus on: did the concept actually show up the way she expected?

sections.title: Learn
sections.content: Two frameworks in depth. The AI confidence spectrum: five levels from silent to assertive, with a real product example at each level. The human-override pattern: when to surface a manual escape hatch, and three ways to do it without making users feel like they're fighting the AI.

sections.title: Discuss
sections.content: Take a product from last week's homework. Run it through the confidence spectrum — where does it sit? Does it use the human-override pattern? Where does it fall short? Pairs annotate together, then report back.

sections.title: Wrap-up
sections.content: Agree on the task for next time and who leads the next session.

sessions.homework: Apply the AI confidence spectrum to your portfolio product. Mark every touchpoint where the system expresses confidence — or should. Bring a marked-up screenshot.

sessions.title: Hands-On Workshop
sessions.goal: build a working prototype that demonstrates at least one AI design pattern
sessions.preMaterials: Bring your marked-up screenshot from last week in a format you can share on screen. No new prep needed — the work you already did is the material.

sections.title: Check-in
sections.content: Go around: each person says in one sentence what she did since last time.

sections.title: Last week's task
sections.content: Marked-up screenshots on screen. Two minutes each — walk through one touchpoint you marked and why. The group picks the most interesting one to redesign together.

sections.title: Learn
sections.content: Live redesign of the screenshot the group chose. The leader drives, everyone contributes. Apply the confidence spectrum and the override pattern. Work through three iterations in 25 minutes.

sections.title: Discuss
sections.content: The group votes on the two changes from the redesign that would have the most impact. What would we do differently with 2 more hours?

sections.title: Wrap-up
sections.content: Agree on the task for next time and who leads the next session.

sessions.homework: Take the redesign we did together and apply it to your own product. One screen, one specific change, same framework. Share a before/after — doesn't have to be polished.

sessions.title: Guest Expert Session
sessions.goal: evaluate an expert's approach and extract two insights to bring into our own work
sessions.preMaterials: Look up the guest's work before the session (link in resources). Write one specific question — something you can't google and that only someone who built it could answer.

sections.title: Check-in
sections.content: Go around: each person says in one sentence what she did since last time.

sections.title: Last week's task
sections.content: Before/afters on screen. Two minutes each. Focus on what changed and what the framework forced you to notice.

sections.title: Learn
sections.content: Guest walks through a project from brief to shipped: what the AI was supposed to do, what actually happened in testing, and the two design decisions that made the difference. Leave 10 minutes for the prepared questions.

sections.title: Discuss
sections.content: What surprised you about how the guest handled the hardest part of the project? Each pair picks one thing to steal and applies it to their own work.

sections.title: Wrap-up
sections.content: Agree on the task for next time and who leads the next session.

sessions.homework: Take one idea from the guest's talk and apply it to something you're working on. Document the before and after in a slide or a written note.

sessions.title: Mid-Program Review
sessions.goal: give structured peer feedback on three projects using the rubric from session 3
sessions.preMaterials: Skim your notes or deliverables from sessions 1–5. Flag one thing you feel confident about and one thing you're still not sure how to use.

sections.title: Check-in
sections.content: Go around: each person says in one sentence what she did since last time.

sections.title: Last week's task
sections.content: Guest follow-up: who applied something from the last session? Share what you tried, even if it didn't work.

sections.title: Learn
sections.content: Look back at sessions 1–5 together. The leader maps the concepts on a whiteboard. The group votes on which ones landed cleanly and which are still fuzzy. Spend the last 15 minutes on the two fuzziest ones.

sections.title: Discuss
sections.content: Each person answers: what is the one thing from the first half you are actually using in your work? What is still abstract? Be specific — name a screen or a decision, not a concept.

sections.title: Wrap-up
sections.content: Agree on the task for next time and who leads the next session.

sessions.homework: Write a 5-sentence brief for your project: what you're designing, what AI challenge it solves, what you've already tried, and what you're still figuring out. This becomes your working brief for the second half.

sessions.title: Advanced Techniques
sessions.goal: apply at least one advanced technique to refine an existing design from an earlier session
sessions.preMaterials: Read your project brief from last session. Come with one specific interaction where the AI output can be wrong and there's currently no recovery designed for it.

sections.title: Check-in
sections.content: Go around: each person says in one sentence what she did since last time.

sections.title: Last week's task
sections.content: Briefs on screen. Two minutes each — read it aloud, then one clarifying question from the group.

sections.title: Learn
sections.content: Three advanced patterns. Streaming UX: how to design for outputs that arrive word by word without making users feel they're watching a typewriter. Error recovery: how to surface when the AI got it wrong without destroying trust. Designing for model updates: how to build interfaces that don't break when the underlying model changes.

sections.title: Discuss
sections.content: Which of the three patterns applies most to your project right now? Pairs sketch one specific change they could make this week — a note, a rough wireframe, a decision.

sections.title: Wrap-up
sections.content: Agree on the task for next time and who leads the next session.

sessions.homework: Pick one of the three patterns and implement or prototype it in your project. Bring a working prototype or annotated mockup — doesn't need to be pixel-perfect.

sessions.title: Real-World Case Studies
sessions.goal: diagnose what worked and what failed in two real AI product launches
sessions.preMaterials: Think of an AI product launch you remember — one that impressed you or one that flopped. Come ready to say what happened and why you think it did.

sections.title: Check-in
sections.content: Go around: each person says in one sentence what she did since last time.

sections.title: Last week's task
sections.content: Prototypes and mockups on screen. Two minutes each — show the interaction, name the pattern you applied, say what surprised you.

sections.title: Learn
sections.content: Two case studies side by side. Case 1: a product that launched well — walk through the three design decisions that held up under real users. Case 2: a product that didn't — walk through the one decision that looked fine in testing and failed in production.

sections.title: Discuss
sections.content: Take the failed case study. In pairs: identify the one design decision you would have changed, and what you'd have done instead. Then bring it back — does anyone disagree?

sections.title: Wrap-up
sections.content: Agree on the task for next time and who leads the next session.

sessions.homework: Audit your own project against the two case studies: list two decisions you're making that match the successful one, and one that resembles the failure. Three bullet points.

sessions.title: Peer Feedback & Critique
sessions.goal: run a 5-minute critique using the critique format we practiced in session 3
sessions.preMaterials: Prepare a 5-minute presentation of your project: problem, solution, one interaction that uses AI, and one thing you're still unsure about. Practice it once.

sections.title: Check-in
sections.content: Go around: each person says in one sentence what she did since last time.

sections.title: Last week's task
sections.content: Audits on screen. Two minutes each — read the three bullet points, say which failure pattern you spotted in your own work.

sections.title: Learn
sections.content: Structured critique: each project gets 5 minutes of presentation and 5 minutes of feedback using this rubric — clarity of the AI's role, quality of the confidence signal, handling of errors. The leader models the first round.

sections.title: Discuss
sections.content: After all critiques: what pattern of feedback showed up across every project? What is the group still not sure how to solve?

sections.title: Wrap-up
sections.content: Agree on the task for next time and who leads the next session.

sessions.homework: Take the feedback from today and make one specific change to your project. Document what changed and why in a note or a slide. This is your penultimate version.

sessions.title: Final Project & Wrap-Up
sessions.goal: present a complete project that incorporates at least three concepts from this program
sessions.preMaterials: Finish your final project. It should include: the problem, your solution, at least one AI interaction you designed from scratch, and one paragraph on what you learned building it.

sections.title: Check-in
sections.content: Go around: each person says in one sentence what she did since last time.

sections.title: Last week's task
sections.content: Penultimate versions on screen. Two minutes each — what changed since the critique, and what you decided not to change.

sections.title: Learn
sections.content: No new material today. Brief framing of what a finished project demonstrates — then straight into final presentations. Each person gets 8 minutes: 5 to present, 3 for questions.

sections.title: Discuss
sections.content: After all presentations: what did this group get consistently right across projects? What would we do differently in a second run of this Bubble?

sections.title: Wrap-up
sections.content: Agree on the task for next time and who leads the next session.
